claim: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) is a translation-dependent RNA quality-control pathway targeting transcripts such as messenger RNAs harboring premature stop-codons or short upstream open reading frame (uORFs).
source: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) is a translation-dependent RNA quality-control pathway targeting transcripts such as messenger RNAs harboring premature stop-codons or short upstream open reading frame (uORFs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMD function in the field.

claim: About half of the pervasive transcripts are degraded by NMD.
source: Our transcription start sites (TSSs) analysis of Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells deficient for RNA degradation pathways revealed that about half of the pervasive transcripts are degraded by NMD, which provides a fail-safe mechanism to remove spurious transcripts that escaped degradation in the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is supported by TSS analysis data from RNA degradation pathway-deficient cells presented in the manuscript.

claim: NMD provides a fail-safe mechanism to remove spurious transcripts that escaped degradation in the nucleus.
source: Our transcription start sites (TSSs) analysis of Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells deficient for RNA degradation pathways revealed that about half of the pervasive transcripts are degraded by NMD, which provides a fail-safe mechanism to remove spurious transcripts that escaped degradation in the nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pervasive transcripts escaping nuclear degradation are targeted by NMD.

claim: The low specificity of RNA polymerase II TSSs selection generates, for 47% of the expressed genes, NMD-sensitive transcript isoforms carrying uORFs or starting downstream of the ATG START codon.
source: Moreover, we found that the low specificity of RNA polymerase II TSSs selection generates, for 47% of the expressed genes, NMD-sensitive transcript isoforms carrying uORFs or starting downstream of the ATG START codon.
evidence: This is supported by genome-wide TSS analysis data showing transcript isoforms in 47% of genes.

claim: There is a significant bias against in-frame ATGs specifically found at the beginning of genes with downstream TSSs.
source: Despite the low abundance of this last category of isoforms, their presence seems to constrain genomic sequences, as suggested by the significant bias against in-frame ATGs specifically found at the beginning of the corresponding genes and reflected by a depletion of methionines in the N-terminus of the encoded proteins.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ATG distribution in genes with internal TSSs.

claim: There is a depletion of methionines in the N-terminus of proteins encoded by genes with downstream TSSs.
source: Despite the low abundance of this last category of isoforms, their presence seems to constrain genomic sequences, as suggested by the significant bias against in-frame ATGs specifically found at the beginning of the corresponding genes and reflected by a depletion of methionines in the N-terminus of the encoded proteins.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of amino acid composition in N-terminal regions of proteins.

claim: In human cells, roughly 75% of the genome gives rise to RNA transcripts of various length but only an estimated 2% corresponds to protein-coding messenger RNAs (mRNAs).
source: In human cells, roughly 75% of the genome gives rise to RNA transcripts of various length but only an estimated 2% corresponds to protein-coding messenger RNAs (mRNAs) (Djebali et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Djebali et al., 2012.

claim: Hundreds of pervasive non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) were identified in S. cerevisiae in addition to stable ncRNAs.
source: Even in a compact genome such as the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (S. cerevisiae), hundreds of such pervasive non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) were identified in addition to the stable ncRNAs such as transfer RNAs (tRNAs), small nucleolar RNAs (sn(o)RNAs), and ribosomal RNA (rRNAs) (Neil et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2009; van Dijk et al., 2011; Geisler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast ncRNAs are transcribed from nucleosome-free regions (NFRs) present throughout the genome, most often at gene promoters and terminators.
source: Yeast ncRNAs are transcribed from nucleosome-free regions (NFRs) present throughout the genome, most often at gene promoters and terminators, and part of these RNAs represent by-products of divergent transcription initiation (Neil et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neil et al., 2009 and Xu et al., 2009.

claim: Part of pervasive ncRNAs represent by-products of divergent transcription initiation.
source: Yeast ncRNAs are transcribed from nucleosome-free regions (NFRs) present throughout the genome, most often at gene promoters and terminators, and part of these RNAs represent by-products of divergent transcription initiation (Neil et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neil et al., 2009 and Xu et al., 2009.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, degradation-coupled transcription termination of pervasive transcripts relies on the Nrd1-Nab3-Sen1 (NNS) complex.
source: In the yeast S. cerevisiae, degradation-coupled transcription termination of pervasive transcripts relies on the Nrd1-Nab3-Sen1 (NNS) complex, which interacts with the carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) of the RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) phosphorylated on serine 5 and triggers termination upon recognition of short sequences on the nascent RNA (Arigo et al., 2006; Thiebaut et al., 2006; Gudipati et al., 2008; Vasiljeva et al., 2008; Schulz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The NNS complex interacts with the CTD of RNAPII phosphorylated on serine 5.
source: In the yeast S. cerevisiae, degradation-coupled transcription termination of pervasive transcripts relies on the Nrd1-Nab3-Sen1 (NNS) complex, which interacts with the carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) of the RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) phosphorylated on serine 5 and triggers termination upon recognition of short sequences on the nascent RNA (Arigo et al., 2006; Thiebaut et al., 2006; Gudipati et al., 2008; Vasiljeva et al., 2008; Schulz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The NNS complex triggers termination upon recognition of short sequences on the nascent RNA.
source: In the yeast S. cerevisiae, degradation-coupled transcription termination of pervasive transcripts relies on the Nrd1-Nab3-Sen1 (NNS) complex, which interacts with the carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) of the RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) phosphorylated on serine 5 and triggers termination upon recognition of short sequences on the nascent RNA (Arigo et al., 2006; Thiebaut et al., 2006; Gudipati et al., 2008; Vasiljeva et al., 2008; Schulz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Early termination of CUTs is coupled with the recruitment of the TRAMP complex and the Rrp6-containing nuclear RNA-exosome for rapid degradation.
source: Early termination of these transcripts (named CUTs for cryptic unstable transcripts) is coupled with the recruitment of the Trf4-Air2-Mtr4 (TRAMP) complex and the Rrp6-containing nuclear RNA-exosome for rapid degradation (Wyers et al., 2005; Davis and Ares, 2006; Tudek et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wyers et al., 2005; Davis and Ares, 2006; Tudek et al., 2014.

claim: A significant proportion of pervasive transcripts can escape nuclear quality-control and be exported to the cytoplasm where they are targeted for degradation by the cytoplasmic 5′-3′ exonuclease Xrn1.
source: However, a significant proportion of the pervasive transcripts can escape this early nuclear quality-control step and be exported to the cytoplasm where they are targeted for degradation by the cytoplasmic 5′-3′ exonuclease Xrn1 (XUT; van Dijk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Dijk et al., 2011.

claim: In the absence of Xrn1p, the average levels of SUTs and CUTs increase by 7.9-fold and 3.6-fold respectively.
source: Their behavior can be similar, as illustrated by the fact that in the absence of Xrn1p the average levels of SUTs and CUTs increase by 7.9-fold and 3.6-fold respectively (van Dijk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Dijk et al., 2011.

claim: NMD was originally described more than two decades ago as a quality-control pathway targeting for degradation mRNAs containing a premature termination codon.
source: Originally described more than two decades ago as a quality-control pathway targeting for degradation mRNAs containing a premature termination codon (Leeds et al., 1991), NMD is a translation-coupled quality-control pathway affecting cytoplasmic transcripts with restricted coding capacities (for a review see Kervestin and Jacobson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leeds et al., 1991.

claim: NMD targets include mRNAs harboring upstream open reading frames (uORFs).
source: NMD targets include mRNAs harboring 'upstream open reading frames' (uORFs) (He et al., 2003; Arribere and Gilbert, 2013) and unspliced or incorrectly spliced transcripts exported to the cytoplasm (Sayani et al., 2008; Kawashima et al., 2014) accounting for roughly 10–15% of mRNAs in yeast as well as in human cells (Kervestin and Jacobson, 2012 and references therein).
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2003 and Arribere and Gilbert, 2013.

claim: NMD targets include unspliced or incorrectly spliced transcripts exported to the cytoplasm.
source: NMD targets include mRNAs harboring 'upstream open reading frames' (uORFs) (He et al., 2003; Arribere and Gilbert, 2013) and unspliced or incorrectly spliced transcripts exported to the cytoplasm (Sayani et al., 2008; Kawashima et al., 2014) accounting for roughly 10–15% of mRNAs in yeast as well as in human cells (Kervestin and Jacobson, 2012 and references therein).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sayani et al., 2008 and Kawashima et al., 2014.

claim: NMD targets account for roughly 10–15% of mRNAs in yeast as well as in human cells.
source: NMD targets include mRNAs harboring 'upstream open reading frames' (uORFs) (He et al., 2003; Arribere and Gilbert, 2013) and unspliced or incorrectly spliced transcripts exported to the cytoplasm (Sayani et al., 2008; Kawashima et al., 2014) accounting for roughly 10–15% of mRNAs in yeast as well as in human cells (Kervestin and Jacobson, 2012 and references therein).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kervestin and Jacobson, 2012.

claim: The false-discovery rate for TSS identification using the TSS sequencing method is less than 2.5%.
source: After normalization using the S. pombe sequencing reads and removal of the ribosomal DNA ones, these experiments generated 2,844,877 reads when TAP was used compared with 72,435 reads when TAP was omitted. The ratio between these two numbers provides an upper limit for the false-discovery rate of TSS identification of 2.5%.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data comparing TAP-treated and untreated samples.

claim: Genome-wide, 77% of the reads obtained for TAP-treated samples could be mapped within a 200 nucleotide region upstream of the start codons with a maximum at around 30 nucleotides upstream from ATGs.
source: Analysis of the cumulative 5′-end read counts per nucleotide around the start codon for all protein-coding genes showed that, genome-wide, 77% (2,190,211) of the reads obtained for TAP-treated samples could be mapped within a 200 nucleotide region upstream of the start codons with a maximum at around 30 nucleotides upstream from ATGs, while only 22% mapped to the same region when this treatment was omitted (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between two independent biological replicates for wild-type cells is 0.89.
source: The Pearson's correlation value (ρ) between the read counts of the 174,151 TSSs identified in the two data sets is indicated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with the correlation coefficient indicated.

claim: The TSS consensus sequence in S. cerevisiae is A(N)6PyPu.
source: Analysis of the TSSs and their surrounding sequences using the Web-LOGO algorithm (Crooks et al., 2004) identified a consensus sequence around TSSs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) similar to the previously reported one derived from a smaller data set (Zhang and Dietrich, 2005). In particular, we observed a very strong bias to start at a purine (88% of mapped TSSs), usually following a pyrimidine (76% of the mapped TSSs), and the enrichment for an A at position −8 relative to the TSS (A(N)6PyPu consensus).
evidence: This is supported by Web-LOGO analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and comparison to Zhang and Dietrich, 2005.

claim: 88% of mapped TSSs start at a purine.
source: In particular, we observed a very strong bias to start at a purine (88% of mapped TSSs), usually following a pyrimidine (76% of the mapped TSSs), and the enrichment for an A at position −8 relative to the TSS (A(N)6PyPu consensus).
evidence: This is calculated from the TSS sequencing data.

claim: 76% of mapped TSSs have a pyrimidine preceding the purine at the TSS.
source: In particular, we observed a very strong bias to start at a purine (88% of mapped TSSs), usually following a pyrimidine (76% of the mapped TSSs), and the enrichment for an A at position −8 relative to the TSS (A(N)6PyPu consensus).
evidence: This is calculated from the TSS sequencing data.

claim: 58% of TSS reads starting with a pyrimidine when aligned on the genome show a mismatch at their first nucleotide, most of the time an A instead of the encoded pyrimidine.
source: Surprisingly, 58% of TSS reads starting with a pyrimidine when aligned on the genome (12% of the mapped TSSs) show a mismatch at their first nucleotide, most of the time an A instead of the encoded pyrimidine (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is observed in the sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 17,812 TSSCs were identified in the study.
source: This analysis allowed us to identify 17,812 TSSCs, among which 5927 could be assigned to 5′-ends of mRNAs corresponding to 5231 ORFs (O category in Supplementary file 1), as previously defined (Pelechano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is the result of peak-calling analysis on the TSS sequencing data.

claim: 5927 TSSCs could be assigned to 5′-ends of mRNAs corresponding to 5231 ORFs.
source: This analysis allowed us to identify 17,812 TSSCs, among which 5927 could be assigned to 5′-ends of mRNAs corresponding to 5231 ORFs (O category in Supplementary file 1), as previously defined (Pelechano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is the result of TSSC assignment to annotated features.

claim: 79% of CUT-TSSCs were significantly stabilized in the absence of Rrp6.
source: In contrast to mRNA-TSSCs, the majority of which were unaffected in the absence of Upf1, Rrp6 or both (Figure 2A) and, as expected (Wyers et al., 2005), CUT-TSSCs were strongly stabilized in the absence of Rrp6 (Figure 2B; 79% stabilized significantly, as determined using the moderated estimation of fold change and dispersion function of DESeq2—Love et al., 2014; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is determined by DESeq2 analysis of the TSS sequencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only 23% of CUT-TSSCs increased significantly in the absence of Upf1.
source: In contrast, only 23% of the CUT-TSSCs increased significantly in the absence of Upf1.
evidence: This is determined by DESeq2 analysis of the TSS sequencing data.

claim: 28% of XUTs and SUTs were significantly stabilized in the absence of Rrp6.
source: The opposite situation was observed for XUTs and SUTs, which were more sensitive to the cytoplasmic NMD quality-control pathway (28% vs 52% significantly stabilized in the absence of Rrp6 or Upf1, respectively; Figure 2C,D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is determined by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: 52% of XUTs and SUTs were significantly stabilized in the absence of Upf1.
source: The opposite situation was observed for XUTs and SUTs, which were more sensitive to the cytoplasmic NMD quality-control pathway (28% vs 52% significantly stabilized in the absence of Rrp6 or Upf1, respectively; Figure 2C,D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is determined by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: 39% of pervasive transcripts (CUTs, SUTs and XUTs) were significantly sensitive to the absence of Upf1 in a wild-type background.
source: Collectively, 39% and 54% of the pervasive transcripts (CUTs, SUTs and XUTs) were significantly sensitive to the absence of Upf1 in a wild-type or rrp6∆ background, respectively, indicating that NMD targets about half of the pervasive transcripts.
evidence: This is calculated from the DESeq2 analysis of all pervasive transcript categories.

claim: 54% of pervasive transcripts (CUTs, SUTs and XUTs) were significantly sensitive to the absence of Upf1 in an rrp6∆ background.
source: Collectively, 39% and 54% of the pervasive transcripts (CUTs, SUTs and XUTs) were significantly sensitive to the absence of Upf1 in a wild-type or rrp6∆ background, respectively, indicating that NMD targets about half of the pervasive transcripts.
evidence: This is calculated from the DESeq2 analysis of all pervasive transcript categories.

claim: In the upf1∆rrp6∆ double mutant, 76% of XUTs/SUTs were significantly stabilized.
source: In the double mutant, 76% and 92% of the XUTs/SUTs and CUTs, respectively, were significantly stabilized, suggesting that NMD provides a fail-safe control mechanism for pervasive transcripts that escaped degradation in the nucleus, reminiscent of what has been previously shown for some unspliced pre-mRNAs (Sayani and Chanfreau, 2012).
evidence: This is determined by DESeq2 analysis of the double mutant data.

claim: In the upf1∆rrp6∆ double mutant, 92% of CUTs were significantly stabilized.
source: In the double mutant, 76% and 92% of the XUTs/SUTs and CUTs, respectively, were significantly stabilized, suggesting that NMD provides a fail-safe control mechanism for pervasive transcripts that escaped degradation in the nucleus, reminiscent of what has been previously shown for some unspliced pre-mRNAs (Sayani and Chanfreau, 2012).
evidence: This is determined by DESeq2 analysis of the double mutant data.

claim: XUTs and SUTs carry spurious ORFs.
source: Indeed, all XUTs and SUTs carry spurious ORFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and some of them have been identified in ribosomal profiling experiments and shown to encode short peptides (Ingolia et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown by analysis of XUT and SUT sequences in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Some XUTs and SUTs have been identified in ribosomal profiling experiments and shown to encode short peptides.
source: Indeed, all XUTs and SUTs carry spurious ORFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and some of them have been identified in ribosomal profiling experiments and shown to encode short peptides (Ingolia et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ingolia et al., 2009 and Smith et al., 2014.

claim: XUTs and SUTs carry, on average, much shorter ORFs and longer 3′-UTRs than mRNAs.
source: Assuming that the first encountered ORF is translated, XUTs and SUTs carry, on average, much shorter ORFs and longer 3′-UTRs than mRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by comparative analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The presence of both a long 3′-UTR and a short ORF increases NMD efficiency in budding yeast.
source: The presence of both a long 3′-UTR and a short ORF increases NMD efficiency in budding yeast (Decourty et al., 2014) and thus explain why these transcripts are efficiently targeted for degradation by this pathway.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Decourty et al., 2014.

claim: XUTs and SUTs found not to be sensitive to NMD have on average significantly shorter 3′-UTRs.
source: Furthermore, the few XUTs and SUTs found not to be sensitive to NMD have on average significantly shorter 3′-UTRs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), which is in agreement with the recently published observation that, in ribosomal profiling experiments, the length of RNA downstream of the ribosome protected region is significantly longer for NMD-sensitive compared with NMD-insensitive unannotated RNA transcripts (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and supported by citation to Smith et al., 2014.

claim: 7739 TSSCs could not be assigned to previously annotated transcripts and were only detected in mutant cells.
source: Amongst the 17,812 TSSCs identified in this study, 7739 could not be assigned to previously annotated transcripts (ORFs, stable ncRNAs or pervasive transcripts) and were only detected in mutants cells (Figure 4).
evidence: This is the result of TSSC assignment analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: 3011 'intergenic-TSSCs' originating from 1843 intergenic regions were identified.
source: These newly identified transcripts, expressed at low levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), originated from intergenic regions (3011 'intergenic-TSSCs' originating from 1843 intergenic regions) as well as from within mRNA transcribed regions either in sense (2978 'B-TSSCs' within 1889 mRNAs) or in antisense orientation (1750 'A-TSSCs' antisense to 1186 mRNAs; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is the result of TSSC classification analysis.

claim: 2978 'B-TSSCs' within 1889 mRNAs were identified.
source: These newly identified transcripts, expressed at low levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), originated from intergenic regions (3011 'intergenic-TSSCs' originating from 1843 intergenic regions) as well as from within mRNA transcribed regions either in sense (2978 'B-TSSCs' within 1889 mRNAs) or in antisense orientation (1750 'A-TSSCs' antisense to 1186 mRNAs; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is the result of TSSC classification analysis.

claim: 1750 'A-TSSCs' antisense to 1186 mRNAs were identified.
source: These newly identified transcripts, expressed at low levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), originated from intergenic regions (3011 'intergenic-TSSCs' originating from 1843 intergenic regions) as well as from within mRNA transcribed regions either in sense (2978 'B-TSSCs' within 1889 mRNAs) or in antisense orientation (1750 'A-TSSCs' antisense to 1186 mRNAs; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is the result of TSSC classification analysis.

claim: B-TSSCs were sensitive to upf1∆ and almost not affected by the deletion of RRP6.
source: While 'B-TSSCs' were sensitive to upf1∆ and almost not affected by the deletion of RRP6 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), 'intergenic' and 'A-TSSCs' were affected by the two mutations (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 'Intergenic' and 'A-TSSCs' were affected by both upf1∆ and rrp6∆ mutations.
source: While 'B-TSSCs' were sensitive to upf1∆ and almost not affected by the deletion of RRP6 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), 'intergenic' and 'A-TSSCs' were affected by the two mutations (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absence of both Rrp6 and Upf1 had an additive effect on the accumulation of 'intergenic' and 'A-TSSCs'.
source: Furthermore, the absence of both Rrp6 and Upf1 had an additive effect on the accumulation of these last two classes, as is the case for previously identified pervasive transcripts.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of single and double mutant effects on these transcript classes.

claim: 55% of A-TSSCs were sensitive to Upf1.
source: Importantly, 55% of the A-TSSCs and 40% of the B-TSSCs, whether repressed by Set2 or not, were sensitive to Upf1 (i.e., increased significantly in upf1∆set2∆ compared with set2∆ cells; Figure 6D and Supplementary file 3), revealing NMD to be an important quality-control mechanism to eliminate internally initiated transcripts.
evidence: This is determined by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 40% of B-TSSCs were sensitive to Upf1.
source: Importantly, 55% of the A-TSSCs and 40% of the B-TSSCs, whether repressed by Set2 or not, were sensitive to Upf1 (i.e., increased significantly in upf1∆set2∆ compared with set2∆ cells; Figure 6D and Supplementary file 3), revealing NMD to be an important quality-control mechanism to eliminate internally initiated transcripts.
evidence: This is determined by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 17% of mRNAs-TSSCs showed a significant increase in the absence of Upf1.
source: Consistent with previously reported data (He et al., 2003; Wyers et al., 2005), the effect on mRNAs was larger upon deletion of UPF1 (with 17% of the mRNAs-TSSCs showing a significant increase in the absence of Upf1) than upon deletion of RRP6 and deletion of both genes simultaneously did not show any additive effect (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is determined by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 2A and consistent with He et al., 2003 and Wyers et al., 2005.

claim: Transcript isoforms in which TSSs were followed by uORFs were globally stabilized in the absence of UPF1.
source: Indeed, transcript isoforms in which TSSs where followed by uORFs were, globally, stabilized in the absence of UPF1, while those in which the annotated start codon was the first ATG downstream the TSS were mostly unaffected (Figure 7A, solid lines; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Transcript isoforms in which the annotated start codon was the first ATG downstream the TSS were mostly unaffected by UPF1 deletion.
source: Indeed, transcript isoforms in which TSSs where followed by uORFs were, globally, stabilized in the absence of UPF1, while those in which the annotated start codon was the first ATG downstream the TSS were mostly unaffected (Figure 7A, solid lines; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: For 1129 out of 5231 active genes (22%), a fraction of their transcript isoforms carried at least one uORF and was significantly sensitive to NMD.
source: Yet, for 1129 out of the 5231 active genes (22%), a fraction of their transcript isoforms carried at least one uORF and was significantly sensitive to NMD.
evidence: This is calculated from the analysis of uORF-containing transcript isoforms.

claim: Isoforms carrying more than one uORF appeared even more sensitive to NMD.
source: Isoforms carrying more than one uORF appeared even more sensitive to NMD (Figure 7A), suggesting that the first AUGs of uORFs containing transcripts are not always efficiently used for translation initiation, likely because they are not in a favorable context (Arribere and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and supported by citation to Arribere and Gilbert, 2013.

claim: 64% of expressed genes (3327 genes) have iTSSs.
source: We considered genes as having iTSSs (3327 genes; 64% of the expressed genes) if they contained at least four iTSS reads, which accounted for 99% of all iTTS reads.
evidence: This is calculated from the iTSS analysis with a threshold of at least four reads.

claim: A fraction of transcript isoforms initiated at iTSSs followed by an out-of-frame ATG and significantly stabilized in the absence of Upf1 could be identified for 1821 out of 5231 expressed genes (35%).
source: A fraction of transcript isoforms initiated at iTSSs followed by an out-of-frame ATG and significantly stabilized in the absence of Upf1 could be identified for 1821 out of the 5231 expressed genes (35%, Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is determined by analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The mean expression level of iTSSs significantly increased in the upf1∆ strain relative to the wild-type.
source: In contrast to the weak overall effects observed for TSSs located directly upstream of the start codon, the mean expression level of iTSSs significantly increased in the upf1∆ strain relative to the wild-type (Figure 7C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transcript isoforms significantly stabilized in NMD-deficient cells were found in 2437 genes (47% of the 5231 expressed genes).
source: Altogether, transcript isoforms significantly stabilized in NMD-deficient cells, either because they carry a uORF or because they initiated at an out-of-frame iTSS, were found in 2437 genes; that is, 47% of the 5231 expressed genes.
evidence: This is calculated by combining genes with uORF-containing and iTSS-initiated NMD-sensitive isoforms.

claim: In transcripts initiated at iTSSs, the first encountered ATGs are most of the time out-of-frame relative to the main ORF.
source: In transcripts initiated at iTSSs, the first encountered ATGs are most of the time out-of-frame relative to the main ORF (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown by analysis in Figure 8A.

claim: There is a bias towards out-of-frame ATGs specifically observed at the beginning of genes for which iTSSs were identified.
source: This bias towards out-of-frame ATGs was specifically observed at the beginning of genes for which iTSSs were identified (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is shown by analysis in Figure 8B,C.

claim: There is a significantly lower frequency of methionine in the N-terminal part of proteins from genes with iTSSs.
source: This correlated with a significantly lower frequency of methionine in the N-terminal part of the corresponding proteins (Figure 8D), even though methionines were found to be globally underrepresented at the beginning of all yeast proteins.
evidence: This is shown by analysis in Figure 8D.

claim: Methionines were found to be globally underrepresented at the beginning of all yeast proteins.
source: This correlated with a significantly lower frequency of methionine in the N-terminal part of the corresponding proteins (Figure 8D), even though methionines were found to be globally underrepresented at the beginning of all yeast proteins.
evidence: This is observed in the amino acid composition analysis.

claim: The TSS sequencing method includes a biotin purification step and allows the selective enrichment of the 5′-ends of capped transcripts.
source: To identify TSSs genome-wide and with high specificity we used a modified genomic 5′-RACE approach (Hashimoto et al., 2009; Arribere and Gilbert, 2013) that we called TSS sequencing, which involves a biotin purification step and allows the selective enrichment of the 5′-ends of capped transcripts (see Figure 1A and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown schematically in Figure 1A.

claim: The TSS sequencing method is based on a modified genomic 5′-RACE approach.
source: To identify TSSs genome-wide and with high specificity we used a modified genomic 5′-RACE approach (Hashimoto et al., 2009; Arribere and Gilbert, 2013) that we called TSS sequencing, which involves a biotin purification step and allows the selective enrichment of the 5′-ends of capped transcripts (see Figure 1A and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hashimoto et al., 2009 and Arribere and Gilbert, 2013.

claim: The consensus sequence for iTSSs was not different from the general consensus sequence for RNAPII transcription initiation.
source: The consensus sequence for the iTSSs was not different from the general consensus sequence for RNAPII transcription initiation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by Web-LOGO analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genes with iTSSs are significantly depleted of in-frame ATGs relative to all ATGs in the first 100 nucleotides when compared with genes without iTSSs (p-value = 3.13 × 10−5).
source: Genes with iTSSs reads are significantly depleted of in-frame ATGs relative to all ATGs in the first 100 nucleotides when compared with genes without iTSSs reads (p-value = 3.13 10−5; ANOVA).
evidence: This is shown by statistical analysis in Figure 8B with ANOVA test.

claim: The A-TSSCs and B-TSSCs more sensitive to Set2 were located further away from the mRNA 5′-ends.
source: In agreement with the observed enrichment in Set2-catalyzed H3K36 methylation towards the 3′ end of ORFs (Pokholok et al., 2005), the 'A' and 'B' TSSCs more sensitive to Set2 were located further away from the mRNA 5′-ends (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A–C and consistent with Pokholok et al., 2005.

claim: B-TSSs were not associated with a strong NFR but instead showed a weak NFR surrounded by two well-positioned nucleosomes.
source: However, unlike the TSSs associated with other features identified in this study, the 'B' TSSs were not associated with a strong NFR (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). Instead, analysing the nucleosome density around these TSSs revealed the presence of a weak NFR surrounded by two well-positioned nucleosomes.
evidence: This is shown by nucleosome density analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The particular nucleosome pattern around B-TSSs might explain their high sensitivity to mutations affecting chromatin structure, such as the deletion of Set2.
source: This particular pattern might explain the high sensitivity of 'B' TSSs to mutations affecting chromatin structure, such as the deletion of the Set2 histone methyl-transferase (Smolle and Workman, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the nucleosome pattern observation and supported by citation to Smolle and Workman, 2013.
